segments.title: Royal Navy plans and command arrangements in 1939
segments.body: The lecture answers a recurring claim that the Royal Navy entered 1939 passive, unprepared, and blind to air power. Readiness here is measured through planning and command arrangements as well as visible ships. Procurement was covered in a separate lecture, leaving strategy, organization, and deployment as the focus. The later examples test the idea that the Navy had done nothing before the war.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the lecture as a rebuttal to claims that the Royal Navy lacked plans, preparation, or awareness of air power in 1939.

segments.summary: Royal Navy readiness in 1939 included planning and air-power awareness that a simple fleet count can miss.

segments.title: Global communications and the Royal Navy's night-fighting edge
segments.body: The British Empire depended on maritime communications that could be attacked almost anywhere. Protecting those sea lanes required dispersed forces to combine without stripping every local station. Night fighting offered an offset to that geographic exposure. The Fleet Air Arm's night attack at Taranto demanded skills the Japanese force did not use in its larger daylight strike on Pearl Harbor. The comparison treats interwar preparation as a search for advantages that raw fleet totals could miss.

evidence.note: The transcript links imperial maritime communications to grand strategy and describes night fighting as a Royal Navy advantage.

segments.summary: Britain's exposed imperial sea routes made night fighting a practical offset to the demands of global protection.

segments.title: HMS Gurkha, imperial identity, and convoy defence
segments.body: The Tribal-class name HMS Gurkha linked a prominent warship with one of the peoples of the British Empire. The example then moves from imperial symbolism to convoy duty: Gurkha charged an air attack aimed at merchant ships. The destroyer was lost, but the aircraft did not reach the less-protected convoy. Convoy defence gave practical force to the broader strategy of holding imperial communications together.

evidence.note: The transcript links the Gurkha name to imperial pride and describes the destroyer's loss while stopping an air attack from reaching a convoy.

segments.summary: HMS Gurkha connects Tribal-class naming and imperial identity with the destroyer's fatal defence of vulnerable merchant ships from air attack.

segments.title: Merchant shipping, naval commands, and a mechanized army
segments.body: Merchant ships above roughly 3,000 tons carried much of Britain's trade and handled long-range movement, which made them prime targets for raiders such as Admiral Graf Spee. A fully mechanized army was mobile on land but harder to ship because its vehicles and equipment required more complicated loading and support. The command map places the densest traffic inside smaller, busier naval areas. Those boundaries indicate advance planning for convoy control and emergency trade protection.

evidence.note: Merchant tonnage, mechanized-force transport, and command boundaries designed around trade routes.

segments.summary: A map of large merchant ships explains why trade protection, convoy organization, and transporting Britain's mechanized army drove Royal Navy command planning.

segments.title: Regional expertise in Royal Navy command
segments.body: The Royal Navy expected the Mediterranean and Far East to demand the most difficult responses, while it kept contingencies for several possible opponents. The China Station commander was unusually senior because reinforcements could quickly turn a regional posting into a fleet command. Australian, New Zealand, and East Indies commands might also come under that officer in war. Repeated overseas postings produced officers who knew local ports, governments, and diplomats before a crisis began. Henry Harwood and British officials in South America illustrate how that accumulated knowledge supported the Battle of the River Plate.

evidence.note: The transcript explains senior overseas commands, recurring postings, and accumulated local knowledge in South America and the Far East.

segments.summary: Senior commands and repeated overseas postings built deep local knowledge in the Far East and South Atlantic.

segments.title: Henderson's convoy theory and the creation of carrier command
segments.body: Reginald Henderson was an influential naval theorist before his better-known work on the Fleet Air Arm. He produced the paper behind the Royal Navy's convoy system, although Jellicoe withheld Henderson's name to protect his career from hostile reaction. Henderson later wrote that the service needed a Rear Admiral, Aircraft Carriers, then nominated himself for the new command. His theory took institutional form through staff papers, appointments, and operational systems instead of one famous published book.

evidence.note: The transcript credits Henderson with the convoy paper and describes how he argued for, then took, the new Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers post.

segments.summary: Henderson's convoy paper and successful bid for a carrier command put naval theory into institutional practice.

segments.title: Henderson's engineering case for naval control of aviation
segments.body: Henderson opposed divided control of naval aviation on technical grounds. An RAF focused on multi-engine bombers was also neglecting its own single-engine fighters, so it was unlikely to prioritize powerful carrier aircraft. After the Navy recovered control of the Fleet Air Arm, Henderson ordered the Sabre and Griffon engine programmes, whose power later served British wartime aviation more broadly. The Fairey Swordfish and Fairey Albacore show the carrier requirement clearly. The lighter Swordfish combined generous wing area with useful power for its mass, while the Albacore's compromises left it short of power. A torpedo aircraft had to lift a heavy weapon from a short deck, making power-to-weight ratio an operational requirement. Henderson made the institutional case legible to politicians by tying control to a specific engineering problem.

evidence.note: The transcript gives Henderson's technical case against RAF control, the Sabre and Griffon orders, and the Swordfish-Albacore power-to-weight comparison.

segments.summary: Henderson connected naval control of the Fleet Air Arm with the engineering priority given to powerful single-engine aircraft.

segments.title: Henderson's shipyard knowledge and maintainable warship design
segments.body: A design dispute began with the First Sea Lord's objection that a larger destroyer would require too many sailors. Henderson answered that extra internal space made machinery easier to reach and maintain. Better access reduced the manpower needed for upkeep, allowing the larger ship to operate with a smaller complement than the J class. Displacement and crew size therefore depended on maintainability as well as hull dimensions.

evidence.note: The transcript presents Henderson's argument that easier access to components would reduce maintenance demands and permit a smaller crew.

segments.summary: Henderson answered objections to a larger destroyer by showing how accessible machinery could reduce maintenance work and crew requirements.

segments.title: Henderson's lost wartime leadership and joint-service politics
segments.body: Henderson died in 1940, before wartime results could secure his place in many postwar accounts. Andrew Cunningham regarded him as a prospective Mediterranean successor and remained in command longer because no equally suitable replacement was available. Mediterranean command required political skill with the Army, RAF, and government as well as fleet tactics. Henderson had already shown that skill by making an engineering case for naval control of the Fleet Air Arm. He also secured HMS Unicorn by presenting the carrier as the mobile support ship required for distant operations.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Henderson's death, Cunningham's succession concerns, interservice politics, HMS Unicorn, and the engineering case for naval aviation control.

segments.summary: Henderson's death in 1940 removed a planned senior successor whose political skill had already secured the Fleet Air Arm and HMS Unicorn.

segments.title: Henderson's shipyard intelligence and practical naval innovation
segments.body: Henderson regularly visited shipyards and learned their construction capacity at first hand. In one meeting he corrected company directors by naming the welding system and number of welders in their own yard. That practical knowledge made inflated estimates of cost or difficulty harder to sustain. The episode also broadens the category of naval theorist: many Royal Navy admirals expressed their ideas through ships and administration instead of polished essays. Henderson worked within that institutional tradition of building arguments into the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Henderson's shipyard visits, knowledge of welding capacity and labor, and the Royal Navy tradition of admirals implementing ideas through construction.

segments.summary: Regular yard visits gave Henderson enough knowledge of welding systems and labor to challenge shipbuilding estimates and turn ideas into ships.

segments.title: Naval treaties, total tonnage, and the division of fleet roles
segments.body: The Washington and London treaty systems imposed increasingly detailed limits on fleet planning. Their rules shaped what each category of warship could contribute. Total cruiser tonnage was the central constraint for Royal Navy planners, with the cap on one ship only part of the problem. Scarcity encouraged heavy destroyers to take fleet work while full-sized cruisers remained available for distant stations, where endurance and diplomatic facilities mattered.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces successive treaty restrictions and emphasizes total cruiser tonnage as a Royal Navy planning constraint.

segments.summary: Successive naval treaties made total cruiser tonnage a central constraint, shaping how the Royal Navy divided work between cruisers and heavy destroyers.

segments.title: A French Indochina contingency that required a larger navy
segments.body: A French contingency for a Japanese attack on Indochina depended on France rapidly doubling the size of its navy. That requirement is difficult to reconcile with the increasingly restrictive treaty environment. The plan is known here only through an English translation of uncertain quality. The apparent force-planning gap therefore remains provisional.

evidence.note: The transcript describes a French Indochina contingency premised on rapidly doubling the navy and explicitly cautions that the source was read in translation.

segments.summary: A French contingency for Japanese aggression in Indochina required a rapid naval expansion that sat uneasily within treaty limits.

segments.title: Tribals, Battle-class destroyers, and Darings in the cruiser role
segments.body: The Tribal class took cruiser-like work with the Home and Mediterranean fleets, freeing scarce cruisers for the Far East and South Atlantic. The wartime Battle class carried the same demand into an emergency hull packed with fighting equipment. Postwar Darings restored room for diplomacy and overseas presence while retaining the heavy-destroyer lineage. A report to Churchill about sending Darings to Syria asked whether they had the accommodation for entertaining and representational duties expected of a cruiser. Royal Navy planners judged a globally deployed ship by its peacetime access and accommodation as well as its weapons.

evidence.note: The transcript traces cruiser-like work from the Tribal and Battle classes to Darings sent to Syria, including the need for diplomatic accommodation.

segments.summary: Heavy destroyers absorbed fleet and presence work so scarce full-sized cruisers could remain on distant stations.

segments.title: Dido, Town, and Type 31: designing space for naval presence
segments.body: The austere Dido class concentrated on fighting, while the larger Town class retained room for presence missions. HMS Birmingham and the slightly larger HMS Belfast make the physical difference visible: a peacetime cruiser needed space for officials, exercises, meals, and other engagements. Representational capacity was nearly as important as combat power for a navy protecting global trade. The same reasoning supports the large Type 31 design, whose spare volume can serve visits, partnership activity, and soft-power work. A compartment that appears empty on a weapons diagram may still carry strategic value.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Dido and Town-class accommodation and applies their presence logic to the Type 31 frigate.

segments.summary: Differences between austere and spacious cruisers explain why Type 31's size matters for diplomacy and global presence.

segments.title: Ark Royal and the two paths of British carrier design
segments.body: Interwar carrier planning offered several possible paths. HMS Ark Royal was a strike carrier built to maximize offensive air power and was conceptually suited to a raid like Taranto. In parallel, the 1936 armored-carrier studies became ancestors of several wartime British carrier classes. Armor addressed Mediterranean air attack, but this account gives greater weight to survival thousands of miles from specialized Far East repair yards. British designers were balancing offensive air-group weight against resilience within a global support system.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Ark Royal's strike role with the 1936 armored-carrier designs and explains their Mediterranean and Far East rationale.

segments.summary: Interwar carrier studies balanced Ark Royal's offensive air-group emphasis against the resilience needed far from British dockyards.

segments.title: Steel flight decks and the logistics of overseas carrier repair
segments.body: Carrier endurance depended on repair materials as well as protection during an attack. Steel plate was easier to stock and move through an overseas support network than the seasoned timber required for a wooden flight deck. Suitable wood needed large storage sheds and careful maintenance before use. Steel construction therefore reduced part of the repair burden for carriers expected to operate far from a major home dockyard.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the storage and transport demands of seasoned wooden flight-deck material with readily stocked steel plate.

segments.summary: Steel flight decks simplified distant repair because steel plate was easier to store and move than the seasoned timber required for wooden decks.

segments.title: The battlecarrier's gun-and-flight-deck employment trap
segments.body: One 1930s hybrid proposal combined Nelson-class battleship guns with an Illustrious-style flight deck. Similar battlecarrier ideas appeared outside the Royal Navy, but the concept created a dangerous employment problem. Heavy guns would tempt commanders to bring the carrier into the battle line, where plunging shellfire could strike its broad deck and central lift. The gunnery role would expose the aviation role to the very risks a carrier should avoid. Adding capabilities to one hull could leave the ship without a coherent way to fight.

evidence.note: The transcript describes a battleship-carrier hybrid and explains how its guns would pull the vulnerable flight deck into surface combat.

segments.summary: Combining battleship guns with a carrier deck risked drawing a vulnerable aviation ship into the battle line.

segments.title: China Station's joint command and headquarters burden
segments.body: The China Station covered a theater so large that a modern map might divide it among three commands. The Army and RAF had no equivalent senior commander there, leaving the naval commander in chief as the effective commander of all British forces in the Far East. That authority required a large wartime staff, perhaps drawn in part from flagship personnel. Regional knowledge therefore had to be backed by a headquarters that could expand before reinforcements arrived.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the command's continental scale, de facto joint authority, large staff requirement, and possible use of flagship personnel.

segments.summary: The China Station commander needed a theater headquarters able to direct other services and absorb a much larger wartime staff.

segments.title: Cruiser commerce raiding as Far East deterrence
segments.body: Before the battle fleet could arrive, the Royal Navy needed to keep Japan uncertain without provoking immediate conflict. As many as fifteen British and Dominion cruisers might be available across the wider Far East. Town- and County-class cruisers designed to hunt surface raiders also had the range and power to raid Japanese trade. Dispersing them would threaten a maritime economy and force the Japanese fleet to protect many routes. The strategy aimed to buy time by making the cost and geography of war difficult to calculate.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the need to buy time, the possible fifteen-cruiser force, and a plan to disperse cruisers against Japanese trade.

segments.summary: A dispersed cruiser threat could buy time by putting Japan's maritime economy at risk before a British battle fleet arrived.

segments.title: HMS Birmingham's Tsingtao showdown
segments.body: In January 1939 Japanese authorities detained a British merchant ship at Tsingtao over alleged aid to China. HMS Birmingham entered the harbor, put a small boarding party aboard the detained vessel, and announced that it would leave the next morning. Three Japanese heavy cruisers trained their guns on Birmingham, which answered by aiming at their bridges. The Japanese ships backed down. The pressure came from the wider cruiser force, since Birmingham's unlocated colleagues could attack Japanese trade elsewhere.

evidence.note: The transcript narrates Birmingham's recovery of the merchant ship, the mutual gun-pointing at Tsingtao, and the wider commerce threat behind the confrontation.

segments.summary: A single light cruiser recovered a detained merchant ship because Japan had to consider what the rest of the British cruiser force might do.

segments.title: HMS Liverpool and the Asama Maru interception
segments.body: In January 1940 HMS Liverpool intercepted the Japanese liner Asama Maru within aircraft range of Japan. The cruiser jammed the liner's communications and removed German merchant seamen trying to return home. The incident provoked Japanese anger and a dispute over its legality. Japan's high command nevertheless had to admit that individual merchant ships could not be protected from British cruisers. Britain promised not to repeat the action, but one liner had already been found and stopped close to Japan without the Japanese fleet preventing it.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Liverpool finding and jamming Asama Maru, removing German seamen, and demonstrating Japanese vulnerability near home waters.

segments.summary: Liverpool's interception of a Japanese liner close to Japan advertised the reach of British economic warfare.

segments.title: Defending Singapore while cruisers attacked Japanese trade
segments.body: Far East planning assigned complementary roles to ships already in the theater. Destroyers and submarines were to protect Singapore and other bases from attack. Cruisers would range outward against Japanese merchant shipping. This paired local defence of the support network with economic pressure on Japan's seaborne trade.

evidence.note: The transcript assigns destroyers and submarines to protect Singapore and other bases while cruisers attack Japanese merchant shipping.

segments.summary: Destroyers and submarines protected Singapore and other bases while cruisers carried economic war toward Japanese merchant shipping.

segments.title: Fuel stockpiles, Singapore, and the infrastructure of Far East war
segments.body: British planning placed enormous fuel reserves in Australia, and those stocks later supported British and American Pacific operations. The reserves show that preparation for a distant war included material infrastructure as well as a reinforcement plan. Singapore was the network's principal prebuilt maintenance harbor. Losing it removed the facility that the Navy expected other services to help defend. Serious logistical preparation could still fail when it depended on joint assumptions and one geographic point.

evidence.note: Australian fuel stockpiles, their later use, and the strategic consequences of losing Singapore.

segments.summary: Prewar fuel storage and the Singapore base show the material preparation behind Far East plans and the consequences of losing their principal dockyard.

segments.title: The Mediterranean Fleet as a planned reinforcement force
segments.body: The Mediterranean posed overlapping risks from Italy, Spain, and potentially France, so prewar plans called for moving the fleet from Malta to Alexandria. Malta advertised British presence in peacetime but was hard to supply and operate as a large wartime base. The force included anti-submarine trawlers and other support vessels suitable for convoy protection or onward movement to the Far East. Battleships and Tribal-class destroyers covered fleet and presence work, allowing cruisers to remain overseas. The Mediterranean Fleet was configured as a reaction force that could leave its home theater.

evidence.note: The transcript covers Malta-to-Alexandria plans, support vessels, cruiser-light force structure, and the Mediterranean Fleet's reinforcement role.

segments.summary: Longstanding plans shifted the fleet from exposed Malta to Alexandria and equipped it to become the first reinforcement force sent east.

segments.title: The Tribal flotilla that nearly crossed Graf Spee's route
segments.body: In September 1939 a Tribal-class flotilla was already south of the Suez Canal. Admiral Graf Spee might have met those destroyers steaming down the African coast if the raider had continued into the Indian Ocean. Graf Spee doubled back, so the interception never occurred. Prewar dispositions had generated an immediate response, yet one change of route decided the outcome of an ocean-wide search.

evidence.note: The transcript places a Tribal flotilla south of Suez and describes its unrealized chance of meeting Graf Spee off Africa.

segments.summary: A destroyer flotilla already south of Suez might have met Graf Spee had the raider continued toward the Indian Ocean.

segments.title: Strategic command versus fleet command in the Far East
segments.body: Sources remain ambiguous about whether a Mediterranean commander bringing the battle fleet east would supersede the China Station commander. The Royal Navy already distinguished tactical fleet command from theater-wide strategic command. One plausible compromise would leave the locally experienced China commander in supreme regional authority while the arriving admiral handled the battle fleet. This arrangement is an interpretation rather than a documented certainty. Reinforcement added a command problem alongside the extra combat power.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses uncertain succession and a possible division between battle-fleet command and supreme strategic command in the Far East.

segments.summary: Reinforcing the Far East raised the question of who commanded the arriving battle fleet and who retained theater-wide authority.

segments.title: Home commands and the overlooked coastal convoy war
segments.body: The Home Fleet theater divided into many commands led by senior admirals. Andrew Cunningham later reduced the structure by asking which headquarters truly needed to join each decision. The wartime network nevertheless coordinated dense flows of merchant ships and convoys around Britain's coast. Those routes came under repeated attack and receive less attention than the Atlantic and Arctic convoys. The concentration of 3,000-ton merchant ships on the command map helps explain why authority was distributed among many smaller coastal areas.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the many home commands, Cunningham's later simplification, and their relationship to dense and vulnerable coastal convoy traffic.

segments.summary: Britain's dense command network coordinated coastal traffic that faced repeated attacks despite receiving less attention than Atlantic and Arctic convoys.

segments.title: Fleet-train ambitions versus merchant-shipping demands
segments.body: The mature American Pacific fleet train should not be projected backward into 1939. Some later American practices followed methods the Royal Navy was already planning, but Britain faced a severe allocation problem. Merchant hulls that could form an emergency naval supply chain were also needed to sustain the national economy and armed forces. Dedicated forward support was therefore harder to create than the plan suggested. Afloat oilers still proved indispensable to Henry Harwood's South Atlantic operations far from a major base.

evidence.note: The transcript compares later American Pacific logistics with British plans, notes competition for merchant hulls, and identifies Harwood's reliance on an oiler.

segments.summary: Britain planned mobile support before the mature American Pacific fleet train, but the same merchant hulls were also needed to supply the country.

segments.title: Self-maintaining cruisers and South Atlantic repair geography
segments.body: Harwood's South Atlantic cruisers operated without a nearby major fleet base and had to handle ordinary maintenance themselves. Proper repairs could require a voyage to Simon's Town, Durban, Freetown, or all the way home. Kingston offered limited facilities and sat uncomfortably close to the neutral United States. The sparse repair map helps explain why the South Atlantic was treated as one large command. Endurance in that theater included maintenance capacity as well as fuel range.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the cruisers self-maintaining and lists the distant South African, West African, and home repair options available to the force.

segments.summary: Long distances to repair yards made self-maintenance a design and deployment requirement for South Atlantic cruisers.

segments.title: Global presence depended on regional and diplomatic knowledge
segments.body: A global navy had to be present before a crisis because a force sailing from home could not solve every distant problem in time. The Army and RAF made different interwar bets; the Navy relied on a worldwide network of ships, commands, and experienced people. Repeated postings produced officers who knew regional ports, governments, and Foreign Office counterparts. Harwood and the diplomat Millington-Drake had a long-standing relationship, and their wives had exchanged letters over years. Global naval deployment worked through an equally global diplomatic service.

evidence.note: The transcript summarizes global presence and uses the long relationship between Harwood, Millington-Drake, and their families to illustrate naval-diplomatic knowledge.

segments.summary: A global fleet had to be deployed before a crisis and connected to diplomats who understood the same regions.

segments.title: Two battleships and the limits of visible deterrence
segments.body: Sending two battleships to Singapore without a carrier offered a weak form of visible deterrence. Against a much larger Japanese battle fleet, the deployment could advertise Britain's immediate ceiling. Dispersed cruisers posed a different problem because they could attack trade and their locations were uncertain. Incidents such as Birmingham at Tsingtao reinforced that threat. A conspicuous concentration could reveal its limit, while mobile forces preserved choices Japan could not easily count.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Churchill's two-battleship deployment with the uncertainty created by dispersed cruisers and possible future fleet reinforcement.

segments.summary: Sending only two battleships to Singapore could advertise Britain's limit, while dispersed cruisers left Japan uncertain about threats to its trade.

segments.title: How South American diplomacy isolated Admiral Graf Spee
segments.body: The South Atlantic cruisers were less powerful than the newest Town class but well suited to repeated port visits and relationship building. German communities in South America might have suggested a useful support network for Admiral Graf Spee. Royal Navy officers and British diplomats had already built enough local goodwill that governments were unwilling to assist the raider. Peacetime presence therefore became wartime isolation. The River Plate campaign depended on diplomatic access to ports as well as the ships that met Graf Spee.

evidence.note: The transcript links South American cruiser visits and diplomatic contacts to the absence of local support for Graf Spee.

segments.summary: Years of cruiser visits and diplomatic relationships helped prevent Graf Spee from finding meaningful support in South America.

segments.title: HMS Ashanti's Freetown visit and the politics of a ship's name
segments.body: The Royal Navy used Tribal-class names to build relationships with the communities those ships claimed to represent. HMS Ashanti visited Freetown and received a silver bell, a golden shield, and ceremonial blessings from the people whose name she carried. The Ashanti king had rebelled against British rule only a few years earlier, giving the ceremony a clear realpolitik dimension. Ashanti later survived the war relatively intact, a result jokingly credited to the blessing. The visit joined warship naming to diplomacy and imperial politics.

evidence.note: Ashanti's Freetown visit, gifts, blessings, and the recent political history behind the ceremony.

segments.summary: Ashanti's visit, gifts, and blessing turned a Tribal-class name into a carefully managed imperial relationship.

segments.title: Eskimo, Nubian, and the Tribal class's combat reputation
segments.body: The Tribals' peacetime symbolism accompanied a conspicuous combat record. HMS Eskimo went through three bows during the Second World War, inspiring the joke that she treated the bow as expendable. HMS Nubian accumulated enough battle honours to be compared with the fleet's most celebrated ships. Ashanti's relatively intact survival offered another form of endurance. Tribal names came to represent damage control, repeated return to service, and wartime prestige as well as imperial ceremony.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Eskimo's repeated bow losses, Nubian's battle honours, and Ashanti's survival as examples of Tribal-class wartime distinction.

segments.summary: Repeated repairs and exceptional battle honours gave the Tribals a wartime reputation alongside their imperial visibility.

segments.title: Why submarines played a different deterrent role
segments.body: Submarines contributed to Royal Navy deterrence without serving the public presence mission at the center of the talk. Their wartime strength depended on concealment. In peacetime they were better suited to intelligence gathering and to creating uncertainty when an opponent knew a patrol existed but could not locate it. Surface ships provided visible reassurance and signaling; submarines supplied a concealed threat.

evidence.note: A submarine question answered through the distinction between covert and visible deterrence.

segments.summary: A closing answer distinguishes the visible diplomatic deterrence of surface ships from the uncertainty and covert value created by submarines.
segments.question: Why were submarines not discussed more in a talk about Royal Navy deterrence?
segments.answerShort: They contributed through covert intelligence and uncertainty, but their effectiveness depended on remaining unseen, so they could not provide the visible presence of cruisers and destroyers.
